name: Optic nerve (CN II)
summary: The optic nerve is not a peripheral nerve but a tract of the central nervous system: the axons of the retinal ganglion cells, myelinated by oligodendrocytes and wrapped in all three meninges with a subarachnoid space, so it swells with raised intracranial pressure (papilledema) and is attacked by multiple sclerosis (optic neuritis). It runs from the optic disc through the orbit and the optic canal to the chiasm, where nasal fibers cross, and continues as the optic tract to the lateral geniculate body, the pretectum and the superior colliculus. Its lesions cause monocular visual loss with a relative afferent pupillary defect, and lesions from the chiasm backward cause binocular field defects.

anatomy.location: Optic disc → intraorbital segment (25 mm, S-shaped to allow eye movement, surrounded by the extraocular muscle cone) → intracanalicular segment (in the optic canal with the ophthalmic artery) → intracranial segment (10 mm, above the cavernous sinus and below the ACA) → chiasm in the suprasellar cistern → optic tract around the cerebral peduncle.

function: Transmission of visual information (acuity, color, fields) from the retina to the lateral geniculate body and visual cortex, and of the afferent limb of the pupillary light reflex to the pretectum.

bestView.label: intraorbital optic nerves converging on the optic canals
optic tracts around the cerebral peduncles to the lateral geniculate bodies

imaging.normalAppearance: The nerve is a cord of intermediate signal within a CSF-filled sheath on coronal fat-saturated T2 (the sheath widens in raised pressure); the chiasm is a flat band above the sella. Optic neuritis shows T2 hyperintensity and enhancement of a segment; meningioma of the sheath enhances around a normal nerve (tram-track).

pathology.finding: Swollen, T2-bright, enhancing segment of the nerve on fat-saturated coronal images; long segments and chiasmal involvement suggest neuromyelitis optica, perineural enhancement suggests MOG antibody disease.
Distended optic nerve sheaths, flattened posterior globes, protrusion of the disc into the vitreous, empty sella.
Tram-track enhancement of the sheath around a non-enhancing nerve with slowly progressive monocular visual loss.
Fusiform enlargement of the nerve, chiasm or tract, often in neurofibromatosis 1.
Optic canal fracture with sudden monocular blindness after frontal trauma.

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: Coronal fat-saturated T2 and T1+Gd of the orbits and chiasm; CT for the canal

lesionEffects.deficit: Monocular visual loss with a relative afferent pupillary defect
Incongruous homonymous hemianopia with a contralateral RAPD
Central scotoma with pain on eye movement and color desaturation
Altitudinal field loss with a swollen pale disc
Enlarged blind spots with preserved acuity

examination: Acuity with correction, color vision (Ishihara or red desaturation), confrontation fields per eye
pearls: An RAPD means an asymmetric lesion in front of the lateral geniculate body: nerve, chiasm or tract. Cortical and geniculate lesions never give an RAPD
Painful monocular loss with a normal disc in a young adult is retrobulbar optic neuritis: think multiple sclerosis

pitfalls: Papilledema is bilateral and painless with preserved acuity early; optic neuritis is usually unilateral and painful with reduced acuity

nuclei.component: SSA relay (retinal ganglion cells are the second-order neurons; the nerve has no brainstem nucleus)

ganglia.name: (none; retinal ganglion cells in the retina)

exit.brainstemExit: Not a brainstem nerve: the optic tract enters the diencephalon at the lateral geniculate body
exit.cisternalCourse: Intracranial segment above the cavernous sinus and diaphragma sellae to the chiasm in the suprasellar cistern; optic tract in the crural and ambient cisterns
exit.foramen: Optic canal of the sphenoid (with the ophthalmic artery), inside the annulus of Zinn
exit.extracranialCourse: Intraorbital nerve within the muscle cone, surrounded by fat and the meningeal sheath, to the back of the globe

branches.name: Optic tract (retinogeniculate fibers)
branches.supplies: lateral geniculate body → optic radiation → calcarine cortex

branches.name: Retinopretectal fibers
branches.supplies: pretectal nuclei for the light reflex

reflexes.name: Pupillary light reflex
reflexes.efferent: oculomotor nerve to sphincter pupillae, both eyes

reflexes.name: Accommodation (near) reflex
reflexes.center: visual association cortex → Edinger–Westphal via the pretectum
reflexes.efferent: oculomotor nerve to ciliary muscle, sphincter pupillae and medial recti

tests.name: Visual acuity
tests.how: Snellen chart with correction, each eye
tests.abnormal: Reduced acuity that does not improve with a pinhole

tests.name: Confrontation fields
tests.how: Compare the patient's field with your own, each eye, all quadrants, with fingers or a red pin
tests.abnormal: Monocular defect (nerve), bitemporal (chiasm), homonymous (tract or beyond)

tests.name: Swinging flashlight test
tests.how: Alternate the light between pupils every 1–2 seconds in dim light
tests.abnormal: The affected pupil dilates when the light swings onto it (RAPD)

tests.name: Fundoscopy
tests.how: Examine the disc margin, color and cup

lesionSigns.localisingValue: optic tract (the only homonymous lesion with a pupil sign)
papilledema (raised pressure) rather than optic neuritis
